Modern enterprise applications demand predictable, ultra-low garbage collection pauses, making traditional stop-the-world collectors like Parallel or CMS inadequate for heaps scaling into hundreds of gigabytes. To solve this, the Java Virtual Machine introduced low-latency garbage collectors known as ZGC (Z Garbage Collector) and Shenandoah, both designed to execute concurrent compaction and mark-sweep phases with pause times that do not scale with the size of the heap. Achieving sub-millisecond or microsecond pauses requires solving a fundamental concurrency challenge: how to move live objects in memory while mutator threads are actively reading and writing to them.

ZGC achieves concurrent compaction primarily through colored pointers and load barriers. By embedding metadata bits directly inside the 64-bit object reference pointer (such as whether an object is marked, finalized, or relocated), ZGC allows hardware-accelerated load barriers to intercept reads and automatically update stale references on the fly. Shenandoah takes a slightly different architectural approach by implementing Brooks pointers (and later shifting to self-healing matrix/indirection implementations), where every object header contains a forwarding address pointer pointing directly to the object's current or new location. When mutator threads access an object, the collector's read and write barriers transparently route through this indirection pointer, ensuring zero application interruption during full-heap compaction.

rows: Colored Pointers (Metadata bits embedded inside the 64-bit reference address)
Brooks Pointers / Indirection (Metadata stored via a dedicated word in the object header)
Load Barriers (Intercepts object reference loads; relies on OS virtual memory page protection tricks historically)
Read/Write Barriers (Intercepts both reads and writes to object fields via explicit forwarding checks)
Historically required uncompressed 64-bit pointers (though modern JDK versions add colored pointer optimizations)
Supports compressed ordinary object pointers (Compressed Oops) in many deployment profiles
Engineered for multi-terabyte heaps with constant-time pause boundaries
Optimized for low-latency across medium-to-large heaps (tens to hundreds of gigabytes)

items: Colored pointers in ZGC utilize unused bits in the 64-bit virtual memory address space (specifically bits 42 through 45 on standard platforms) to store state flags such as Finalizable, Marked0, Marked1, and Remapped. Because these bits are part of the pointer itself, the CPU's memory management unit (MMU) would normally fault unless mapped appropriately, requiring ZGC to map the same physical memory to multiple virtual address spaces.

Brooks pointers in Shenandoah add a self-referencing pointer field directly to the object layout, positioned right before the standard object header. When an object is evacuated during garbage collection, the forwarding pointer of the old object instance is atomically updated to point to the new copy, allowing subsequent mutator accesses to self-heal.

Load barriers in ZGC act inline: when a Java thread loads a reference from the heap, the load barrier checks the color bits of the pointer. If the pointer color indicates the object has been moved or requires marking validation, a slow-path routine is triggered to resolve the correct address and update the reference in place.

parsed_answer.content: A critical production gotcha when deploying ZGC or Shenandoah is memory headroom management. Because both collectors perform compaction concurrently while application threads are actively allocating objects, they require significantly more headroom than a traditional Stop-The-World collector like G1. If your allocation rate exceeds the collection thread throughput, the JVM will fall back to a synchronous stop-the-world full GC cycle, completely neutralizing your latency SLAs. Always provision your heap with at least 20-30% free headroom and tune your allocation stalling thresholds accordingly.
